Carthage
KAR-thij
proper noun (an ancient North African city and church centre)
From the Punic Qart-hadasht (“new city”); the great North African city, refounded as a Roman colony, that became an early centre of Latin Christianity.

📖 Biblical Definition

Carthage was the great city of Roman North Africa that became, in the second through fifth centuries, a chief centre of Latin-speaking Christianity, home to a vigorous and learned church. From its soil came Tertullian, the fierce apologist who shaped the church's Trinitarian vocabulary; Cyprian, the martyr-bishop who wrote on the unity of the church and the duties of bishops; and, nearby, the towering Augustine of Hippo. The dictionary marks Carthage for the church councils held there, which spoke to two matters of lasting weight. First, the Councils of Carthage (notably 397) listed the books received as canonical Scripture, an early witness to the church's recognition—not creation—of the canon; the church did not give the books their authority but received and acknowledged the authority God had stamped upon them. The dictionary honours this witness while holding that the canon of the Old Testament is the Hebrew Scriptures the Jews received and our Lord confirmed, and that the apocryphal books some African lists included are not inspired Scripture but writings of lesser sort. Second, the African church wrestled with the Donatist schism over the holiness of the church and the validity of sacraments administered by unworthy ministers—a controversy answered by Augustine, that the efficacy of the ordinances rests not on the minister's worth but on God's appointment. The dictionary honours Carthage as a fountain of Latin theology and a faithful early witness to the gospel and the Scriptures, while weighing all its councils and fathers, as ever, by the supreme rule of the written Word.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The great North African city and early centre of Latin Christianity; home to Tertullian and Cyprian, and the site of councils that witnessed to the canon of Scripture and wrestled with the Donatist schism—honoured, yet weighed by the Word.

CARTHAGE, proper noun. [Punic Qart-hadasht, “new city.”] A great city of Roman North Africa.

An early centre of Latin-speaking Christianity.

Home of Tertullian and of Cyprian, the martyr-bishop.

The Councils of Carthage witnessed to the books received as Scripture.

The African church wrestled with the Donatist schism over the church's holiness.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Some African canon lists included apocryphal books not truly inspired, and the Donatist schism erred over the church's holiness and the validity of the sacraments; the church recognizes, not creates, the canon, and the ordinances rest on God's appointment.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours Carthage as a fountain of Latin theology and a faithful early witness: home to Tertullian and Cyprian, near to Augustine, and the site of councils that acknowledged the books received as canonical Scripture. The principle to guard here is that the church recognizes the canon, it does not create it. The councils did not confer authority on the Scriptures; they witnessed to the authority God had already stamped upon His inspired Word. Yet some African lists embraced the apocryphal books, which the dictionary, with the Reformers, holds to be writings of lesser sort and not inspired Scripture; the Old Testament canon is the Hebrew Scriptures the Jews received and our Lord confirmed in the law, the prophets, and the psalms.

The African church also faced the Donatist schism, which made the validity of the sacraments and the very being of the church hang upon the worthiness of the minister, so that ordinances administered by the lapsed or unworthy were counted void. Augustine answered rightly that the efficacy of the ordinances rests not on the minister's holiness but on God's appointment, for neither is he that planteth any thing, nor he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase. The dictionary honours the genuine zeal of the African church for purity while naming the Donatist error, and weighs all the councils and fathers of Carthage, as ever, by the supreme and final rule of the written Word.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Punic Qart-hadasht (“new city”); the North African city, refounded by Rome, that became a centre of Latin Christianity and church councils.

Qart-hadasht, Punic, “new city,” the origin of the name Carthage.

A great city of Roman North Africa, centre of Latin Christianity.

Tertullian, the fierce apologist, laboured in its milieu.

Cyprian, the martyr-bishop, wrote on the unity of the church there.

The Councils of Carthage witnessed to the canon of Scripture.

"He held the Councils of Carthage to have recognized, not created, the canon of Scripture."

"She noted Augustine answered the Donatists that the ordinances rest on God's appointment, not the minister's worth."
